[PATH:empirical] Historical panel data on GDP, material footprint, and CO2 emissions from the UN IRP and World Bank (1970-2020) across all countries — Provides direct empirical test of whether absolute decoupling (falling resource use and emissions per unit GDP) has occurred globally over long periods, and whether it is sufficient to keep within planetary boundaries.

[PATH:theoretical] Integrated assessment model simulations (e.g., IMAGE, MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM) under shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs) with explicit planetary boundary constraints — Allows testing of whether decoupling trends projected over 50 years can meet strict ecological limits, or if additional structural changes (e.g., circular economy, demand reduction) are required.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of empirical studies on decoupling (e.g., Haberl et al. 2020, Wiedenhofer et al. 2020) and reviews of planetary boundary compliance — Synthesizes existing evidence on the extent and limits of decoupling, and identifies gaps in linking decoupling rates to specific sustainability targets.

C006.object: achieving strict ecological sustainability targets under planetary boundaries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: long-run decoupling of GDP growth from resource use and environmental impact achieving strict ecological sustainability targets under planetary boundaries]

[PATH:empirical] Historical time-series analysis of global GDP, material footprint, and carbon emissions (e.g., from the UNEP International Resource Panel, World Bank, and Global Carbon Project) to test for absolute decoupling over multi-decadal periods. — Directly assesses whether GDP growth has been accompanied by declining resource use and emissions in absolute terms, which is necessary for staying within planetary boundaries.

[PATH:theoretical] Integrated assessment models (e.g., IMAGE, REMIND, or MESSAGEix) that simulate future GDP growth under strict ecological constraints, incorporating scenarios of technological change and circular economy policies. — Provides forward-looking, quantitative evidence on whether plausible degrees of decoupling can meet planetary boundary targets over the 30-50 year horizon.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of empirical studies on rebound effects and the Jevons paradox in global resource efficiency improvements. — Examines whether efficiency gains from decoupling are systematically offset by increased consumption, undermining the potential for achieving strict sustainability targets.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical analysis of economy-wide material flow accounts (EW-MFA) and GDP data for OECD countries (1950–2020) to test the relationship between relative decoupling rates and subsequent absolute resource use trends, controlling for investment cycles. — Directly tests whether periods of relative decoupling are followed by accelerated absolute resource consumption, as predicted by the rebound effect mechanism.

[PATH:literature] Review of literature on the Jevons paradox and rebound effects in high-income economies, focusing on empirical studies of energy efficiency gains and their reinvestment into production and consumption sectors. — Provides theoretical and empirical grounding for the causal chain from efficiency gains to expanded throughput, which is central to the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Econometric modeling of historical data on GDP, resource use, and planetary boundary indicators (e.g., carbon emissions, land use, material footprint) for high-income economies, using panel vector autoregression to test for feedback loops between decoupling and overshoot. — Allows causal inference on whether relative decoupling amplifies absolute overshoot over time, while accounting for confounding factors like technological change and policy.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of empirical studies on the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) for resource use and emissions, focusing on high-income countries post-1980 — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether technological innovation and efficiency gains lead to absolute decoupling or merely relative decoupling, clarifying the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical analysis of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and its impact on GDP growth vs. emissions intensity, combined with case studies of carbon pricing in jurisdictions with prices near $100/tonne (e.g., Sweden, Switzerland) — Provides real-world data on whether high carbon prices have led to decoupling of GDP from resource use and emissions, and whether such pricing is politically sustainable.

[PATH:theoretical] Integrated assessment models (e.g., IMAGE, GCAM, REMIND) that simulate global carbon pricing at $100/tonne+ and virgin material extraction bans in high-income countries, with sensitivity analysis on technology adoption and rebound effects — Allows testing of the combined policy scenario under varying assumptions about technological change, substitution, and international cooperation, revealing feasibility constraints and potential unintended consequences.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of empirical studies on material footprint decoupling and the effectiveness of extraction bans (e.g., on mining, logging) in high-income nations, including political economy analyses of enforcement and leakage — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether bans alone can drive decoupling, and whether they are politically viable without triggering offshoring of extraction to lower-income regions, which would undermine global decoupling.

C012.subject: long-run decoupling of GDP growth from resource use and environmental impact
C012.object: existing technologies and market-driven innovations without reliance on unproven interventions
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: long-run decoupling of GDP growth from resource use and environmental impact existing technologies and market-driven innovations without reliance on unproven interventions]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term empirical datasets on GDP, material footprint, and carbon emissions (e.g., from the OECD, World Bank, and Global Footprint Network) covering high-income economies over the past 20-30 years — Analyzing trends in decoupling rates (relative and absolute) in countries that have already adopted many existing technologies and market mechanisms can directly test whether observed decoupling is consistent with the hypothesis's claim that it is achievable without unproven interventions.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses and systematic reviews of technology adoption and efficiency gains (e.g., from the IPCC, IRENA, or the Journal of Industrial Ecology) focusing on sectors like energy, manufacturing, and construction — Synthesizing evidence on the actual impact of proven technologies (renewables, circular economy practices, digital optimization) on resource intensity and emissions will reveal whether current innovation rates and diffusion are sufficient for sustained decoupling over the next 20-30 years.

[PATH:theoretical] Integrated assessment models (IAMs) or economy-environment simulation studies that project GDP, resource use, and environmental impacts under scenarios with only currently deployed or commercially viable technologies (e.g., from the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways literature or the Energy Modeling Forum) — These models can test the counterfactual: whether market-driven innovation and existing technologies can produce long-run decoupling without relying on speculative breakthroughs (e.g., negative emissions or novel materials). Comparing model outputs with historical decoupling rates provides a rigorous test of the hypothesis's feasibility.
